task_row_model.query: For which real values of p does the improper integral ∫_{1}^{∞} (ln x)^2 / x^p dx converge? Give a rigorous justification.

documents.content: A basic tool for testing convergence of improper integrals on [1,∞) is the p-test: the integral ∫_{1}^{∞} x^{-p} dx converges exactly when p>1 and diverges otherwise. One often compares a more complicated integrand to x^{-p} to deduce convergence or divergence. If an extra factor grows more slowly than any power of x, comparison may still work, but care is needed: logarithmic factors can alter the borderline cases. The comparison test requires finding a simple majorant or minorant on a tail interval, and verifying integrability directly when possible.

When analyzing integrals over (0,1] with singularities at zero, substitutions like x = e^{-t} are useful. For integrals of the form ∫_{0}^{1} x^{-p} (ln x)^k dx, setting x = e^{-t} transforms the domain to t∈[0,∞) and the integrand to t^k e^{-(1-p)t}. The transformed integral converges for 1-p>0 (i.e. p<1) because polynomial factors t^k are dominated by the exponential decay. This criterion characterizes many integrals with logarithmic weights near zero but addresses behavior at the lower endpoint rather than at infinity.

The special case p = 1 can be analyzed directly. Consider ∫_{1}^{X} (ln x)^2 / x dx. Let u = ln x, so du = dx/x and the integral becomes ∫_{0}^{ln X} u^2 du = (ln X)^3 / 3. Taking X → ∞, (ln X)^3 / 3 → ∞, so the integral diverges for p = 1. This computation shows the logarithmic factor is strong enough to make the p = 1 case divergent, even though the p-test for x^{-p} alone would be inconclusive at the boundary.

Set t = ln x (so x = e^t and dx = e^t dt). Then ∫_{1}^{∞} (ln x)^2 / x^p dx transforms to ∫_{0}^{∞} t^2 e^{-t(p-1)} dt. Convergence of this improper integral depends on the exponential factor e^{-t(p-1)} dominating the polynomial t^2 as t → ∞. The integral ∫_{0}^{∞} t^2 e^{-α t} dt converges precisely when α>0 and equals 2/α^3 by the Gamma function identity Γ(3)=2. Hence the original integral converges if and only if p-1>0, i.e. p>1, and diverges for p ≤ 1.

Oscillatory integrals such as ∫_{1}^{∞} sin x / x dx require different criteria: the Dirichlet test shows conditional convergence when a bounded primitive multiplies a monotone decreasing function tending to zero. Such integrals can converge without absolute convergence; in particular ∫_{1}^{∞} sin x / x dx converges conditionally, while ∫_{1}^{∞} |sin x|/x dx diverges. These methods emphasize cancellation and boundedness rather than comparison with positive monotone kernels and are not directly applicable to non-oscillatory, sign-definite integrands with logarithmic weights.
